stories.headline: Fieldnote runs forty client projects without a status meeting.
stories.summary: A brand and product studio replaced weekly status calls with a shared overview and project pages clients can follow.

quote.text: Everyone opens the overview before they open their inbox. The question “where are we?” simply stopped coming up.

sections.title: The problem
paragraphs: Fieldnote’s leads spent Monday mornings collecting updates from designers and turning them into client reports. By the time a report went out, half of it was out of date.

sections.title: What changed
paragraphs: Every engagement became a Tandem project with an owner, a due date and a task list. Designers tick off tasks as they go, so progress and the activity feed stay current without anyone writing them up.
Leads share saved views with each client team: one for work in review, one for the delivery timeline.

sections.title: The result
paragraphs: Status calls became review sessions about the work itself. Clients see the same timeline the studio sees.

stories.headline: Kiln Coffee opened three cafés in one season.
stories.summary: A roaster and café group planned fit-outs, hiring and launches across three sites from one board.

quote.text: The board showed us which café was stuck before anyone had to say it out loud.

sections.title: The problem
paragraphs: Each new café had its own spreadsheet, and the three spreadsheets never agreed. Contractors, suppliers and the hiring team all worked from different dates.

sections.title: What changed
paragraphs: The operations team set up one project per café and moved them across the board as fit-out, hiring and soft launch finished. Comments with mentions replaced long email threads with suppliers’ contacts.

sections.title: The result
paragraphs: All three sites opened within a week of their planned dates, and the playbook now starts every new site.

stories.headline: Brightpath keeps volunteers and staff on one plan.
stories.summary: A learning nonprofit coordinates a small staff and a rotating group of volunteers without extra tools.

metrics.label: to get a new volunteer started

quote.text: New volunteers find their tasks on the first day. That used to take a week of emails.

sections.title: The problem
paragraphs: Volunteers came and went each term, and every handover lost context: who owned which session, what was left to prepare.

sections.title: What changed
paragraphs: Each programme is a project with tasks assigned to named people. Files keep lesson plans next to the work, and the getting-started list guides new volunteers through their first steps.

sections.title: The result
paragraphs: Handovers take an afternoon. The activity feed shows the next volunteer exactly what happened before them.

stories.headline: Meridian Build sees every site on one timeline.
stories.summary: A mid-sized builder tracks permits, trades and inspections across concurrent sites.

quote.text: The timeline is the first thing our directors look at. Overlaps between trades are obvious weeks ahead.

sections.title: The problem
paragraphs: Site managers reported progress in different formats, so directors could not see where two sites needed the same crew in the same week.

sections.title: What changed
paragraphs: Meridian imported its open sites from a spreadsheet and gave each an owner and a due date. The Timeline view now shows every site side by side, and a saved view filters it to one region.

sections.title: The result
paragraphs: Crew clashes are found in planning rather than on site, and inspections are booked with fewer surprises.

testimonials.text: Our weekly update wrote itself once tasks drove progress.
I stopped asking for status. I just open the project.
Undo on everything means people actually try things.
Saved views gave each client their own window into the work.
Mentions reach the right person, and nobody hunts through email.
Importing our spreadsheet took minutes, problems and all.
